user_text: Compare REST and GraphQL for a small internal API.
assistant_text:
# REST vs GraphQL for a Small Internal API

## Quick Summary

| Aspect | REST | GraphQL |
|--------|------|---------|
| Learning curve | Low | Medium |
| Setup complexity | Low | Medium-High |
| Flexibility | Moderate | High |
| Tooling maturity | Excellent | Good |
| Best fit | Simple, stable resources | Complex, varying data needs |

---

## REST

### How it works
```
GET    /users          → list users
GET    /users/42       → get user
POST   /users          → create user
PUT    /users/42       → update user
DELETE /users/42       → delete user
```

### Pros
- **Simple to understand** — HTTP verbs + URLs are intuitive
- **Easy to test** — curl, Postman, browser work out of the box
- **HTTP caching** works naturally (GET requests)
- **Widely understood** — any new team member knows it
- **Less boilerplate** to get started

### Cons
- **Over-fetching** — endpoint returns fields you don't need
- **Under-fetching** — may need multiple requests for related data
- **Versioning pain** — `/v1/`, `/v2/` sprawl over time

---

## GraphQL

### How it works
```graphql
# Single endpoint: POST /graphql
# Client defines exactly what it needs

query {
  user(id: 42) {
    name
    email
    posts {
      title
    }
  }
}
```

### Pros
- **Fetch exactly what you need** — no over/under-fetching
- **Single endpoint** — no URL management
- **Self-documenting** via introspection and schema
- **Strongly typed schema** catches errors early

### Cons
- **More setup** — schema, resolvers, types required upfront
- **Harder to cache** — POST requests don't cache like GET
- **Overkill overhead** for simple CRUD
- **Error handling** is non-standard (often returns 200 with errors)

---

## Side-by-Side Example

**Fetch a user's name and their post titles**

### REST (2 requests)
```bash
GET /users/42
# Returns: { id, name, email, role, createdAt, ... } ← extra fields

GET /users/42/posts
# Returns: [{ id, title, body, views, ... }] ← extra fields
```

### GraphQL (1 request, exact data)
```graphql
query {
  user(id: 42) {
    name
    posts { title }
  }
}
# Returns exactly: { user: { name: "Alice", posts: [{ title: "..." }] } }
```

---

## For a Small Internal API — My Recommendation

```
Simple CRUD / stable schema / small team  →  REST ✅
Complex queries / multiple consumers      →  GraphQL ✅
```

### Choose **REST** if:
- You have **straightforward resources** (users, orders, products)
- The team is **small and familiar with REST**
- You want to **ship fast** with minimal setup
- Clients are **homogeneous** (one frontend, one use case)

### Choose **GraphQL** if:
- Different clients need **different shapes** of the same data
- You have **deeply nested/related data** (social graph, reporting)
- You want a **self-documenting contract** between teams
- You're building something that will **grow significantly**

---

## Practical Verdict

> For most **small internal APIs**, **REST wins** on simplicity and speed.
> GraphQL pays off when you have **multiple consumers with varying data needs**
> or a **complex domain model** — which small internal APIs often don't have.

Start with REST. Migrate if you feel the pain.

user_text: Give the main difference in one sentence.
assistant_text: **REST uses fixed endpoints that return predefined data, while GraphQL uses a single endpoint where the client specifies exactly what data it needs.**

user_text: Which is simpler to cache and why?
assistant_text: **REST is simpler to cache** because its GET requests map directly to URLs, which HTTP infrastructure (browsers, CDNs, proxies) already knows how to cache automatically — whereas GraphQL typically uses POST requests to a single endpoint, which HTTP caches ignore by default.

user_text: Name one downside of GraphQL for a small team.
assistant_text: **Higher upfront complexity** — a small team must define and maintain a typed schema and write resolvers before getting anything working, which slows initial development compared to simply standing up a few REST endpoints.

user_text: Name one downside of REST for changing requirements.
assistant_text: **Versioning sprawl** — as requirements change, REST APIs tend to accumulate multiple versions (`/v1/`, `/v2/`) or bloated endpoints to accommodate new data needs, making the API harder to maintain over time.

user_text: Which is easier to secure by default?
assistant_text: **REST is easier to secure by default** — standard HTTP security tools (API gateways, rate limiters, firewalls) work naturally with its distinct URLs and methods, whereas GraphQL's single endpoint makes it harder to apply per-operation access control and more vulnerable to expensive nested query attacks without extra tooling.

user_text: Give a short recommendation for a 2-person team.
assistant_text: **Use REST** — a 2-person team should prioritize moving fast over flexibility, and REST's simplicity means less setup, easier debugging, and no learning curve, letting both developers focus on building features rather than managing a schema.

user_text: Provide one thing they have in common.
assistant_text: Both REST and GraphQL **transfer data over HTTP and can return JSON responses**, making them compatible with the same basic client code, authentication headers, and transport-level security (HTTPS).

user_text: State which has clearer tooling out of the box.
assistant_text: **REST has clearer tooling out of the box** — standard tools like curl, Postman, and browser dev tools work immediately with no configuration, whereas GraphQL typically requires specialized clients like GraphiQL or Apollo to get the same level of usability.
**For most small internal APIs, use REST — it's simpler, faster to set up, and easier to maintain unless you have complex, varying data needs.**

- **Choose REST** for simplicity, speed, and ease of maintenance on small internal APIs.
- **Choose GraphQL** only if different clients need different shapes of data or your domain is complex.

REST is simpler, faster to set up, and easier to cache and secure, making it the default choice for small internal APIs — GraphQL is powerful but adds complexity that only pays off when clients have varying or complex data needs.
